title: The Best Place and Time to Have That Conversation
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that the physical setting, timing, and accompanying activity of a conversation shape how openly people communicate just as much as the words exchanged. It contrasts formal, face-to-face settings like conference rooms with side-by-side activities like walking or driving, which lower people's guard and encourage more candid disclosure. The author suggests leaders deliberately vary where and how they hold important conversations, treating the choice of setting as a strategic decision rather than a scheduling afterthought.
points: The setting, timing, and shared activity of a conversation strongly influence how openly people communicate.
Side-by-side activities like walking or driving feel more casual and reduce the pressure people feel to prepare formal responses.
People carry distinct, setting-specific expectations about what should or shouldn't be discussed.
Lowering a leader's perceived status through informal settings tends to increase disclosure from others.
Leaders should treat the choice of location and activity for important conversations as a deliberate strategic decision.
quotes: Where a conversation takes place and what else the parties are doing during the exchange really matters.
Leaders who want to learn more about what others really think select the time, location, and activity that primes the pump for open communication.
Conversations when walking or driving seem more casual and informal because both parties are side-by-side rather than face-on.
This expectation encourages disclosure and diminishes the natural urge to pre-think or prepare to respond as they do in a more formal setting.
The best leaders don’t conduct all of their conversations from behind a desk or in a conference room.
